qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN). Which adult infectious condition is PAN notably associated with?
qs.e: Some cases of Polyarteritis Nodosa, especially in adults, are known to be associated with Hepatitis B infection. The other viruses listed are not highlighted in this context.

ai.title: Polyarteritis Nodosa
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis affecting medium-sized arteries. It causes inflammation and damage to vessel walls, leading to organ dysfunction. Diagnosis relies on clinical features, biopsy, and exclusion of other causes.

sections.p: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic vasculitis characterized by necrotizing inflammation of medium-sized arteries, predominantly affecting the kidneys, heart, liver, and gastrointestinal tract. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring evidence of vasculitis and exclusion of other causes like ANCA-associated vasculitides or infections.
b: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy and exclusion.

t.a: Clinical suspicion based on organ involvement
t.b: Suggests PAN when patients present with multi-system disease (e.g., abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, skin lesions, hypertension, renal insufficiency).

t.a: Artery biopsy (e.g., nerve, muscle, kidney, liver)
t.b: Confirms necrotizing inflammation in a medium-sized artery. A positive biopsy is highly suggestive; a negative biopsy does not exclude PAN if clinical suspicion is high.

t.a: Exclusion of other vasculitides and mimics
t.b: Rules out ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA), connective tissue diseases, infections (e.g., HBV, HIV), and drug-induced vasculitis.

sections.p: Severity is assessed by the number of organs involved and the presence of specific poor prognostic factors. A common staging system considers factors like renal or cardiac involvement, gastrointestinal ischemia, and neurological deficits.
b: Assess organ involvement (kidneys, heart, GI, CNS, skin).
Severity dictates treatment intensity and prognosis.

t.b: Indicates significant renal involvement and risk of severe hypertension and renal failure.

t.a: Evidence of myocardial infarction or heart failure
t.b: Signifies severe cardiac involvement and poor prognosis.
Indicates severe mesenteric vasculitis with high mortality.

sections.p: While the exact cause is often unknown, PAN is frequently associated with Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Other triggers can include other infections, autoimmune dysregulation, or genetic predisposition, though these are less common than HBV.
b: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection (most common identifiable cause).

t.b: Detects current or past HBV infection, a strong trigger for PAN. Positive results strongly suggest HBV-associated PAN.
Rules out HIV, which can also be associated with vasculitis. Negative results help narrow the differential.

sections.p: Presentation is diverse, reflecting the organs affected. Common symptoms include fever, weight loss, myalgias, arthralgias, abdominal pain, hypertension, peripheral neuropathy, and skin lesions like livedo reticularis or ulcers. Renal and gastrointestinal involvement are particularly concerning.

t.b: A mottled, purplish discoloration of the skin, often a sign of underlying vasculitis affecting small vessels supplying the skin.
Assesses for sensory or motor deficits, often asymmetric (mononeuritis multiplex), suggesting nerve ischemia due to vasculitis.
Detects hypertension, which can be severe if renal arteries are involved.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm inflammation, identify organ damage, and exclude other causes. Basic blood tests, imaging, and specific serologies are crucial. Biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis.

t.b: Assesses for anemia (chronic disease, bleeding) or thrombocytosis (inflammation). Elevated white cell count can indicate infection or inflammation.

t.a: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)
t.b: Non-specific markers of inflammation. Elevated levels support active vasculitis but are not diagnostic. Normal levels can occur in active PAN.
Assess for kidney involvement, which is common and can lead to hypertension and renal failure. Elevated urea and creatinine indicate impaired renal function.
Detects liver involvement (e.g., hepatitis) or damage from vasculitis. Abnormalities can indicate hepatic artery or parenchymal involvement.
Checks for proteinuria and hematuria, indicating renal inflammation (glomerulonephritis or interstitial nephritis). Significant findings suggest kidney damage.
Crucial for identifying HBV infection, a common trigger. Positive HBsAg indicates active infection and likely HBV-associated PAN.
Excludes HIV as a cause of vasculitis. Negative results are important for differential diagnosis.
Visualizes medium-sized arteries for aneurysms, stenoses, or occlusions characteristic of PAN. Positive findings strongly support the diagnosis.

t.a: Artery biopsy (e.g., sural nerve, muscle, kidney, liver)
t.b: Confirms necrotizing inflammation in a medium-sized artery. A positive biopsy is diagnostic; a negative biopsy does not rule out PAN if clinical suspicion is high.

sections.p: Urgent attention is needed for signs of impending organ damage. Complications include irreversible organ failure, rupture of aneurysms, gastrointestinal perforation, myocardial infarction, and stroke.
b: Stroke or central nervous system involvement.

t.b: May indicate mesenteric ischemia or bowel infarction, a life-threatening complication requiring urgent surgical assessment.
Suggests rapidly progressing renal artery stenosis, risking acute kidney injury and hypertensive emergency.
Can indicate CNS vasculitis or stroke, requiring urgent investigation and management.

sections.p: Treatment targets inflammation and the underlying cause. Corticosteroids are the mainstay, often combined with immunosuppressants. Antiviral therapy is used for HBV-associated PAN. Supportive care includes blood pressure control and management of organ damage.
b: Treat underlying cause (e.g., antivirals for HBV).

t.b: First-line treatment to reduce inflammation. It suppresses the immune response causing vasculitis.
Used for severe or refractory disease to induce remission and prevent relapses by profoundly suppressing the immune system.
Administered for HBV-associated PAN to suppress viral replication, which is thought to drive the immune complex formation.

t.a: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs)
t.b: Used to control hypertension, especially in cases of renal artery stenosis, and protect kidneys.

sections.p: Regular monitoring for disease activity, treatment toxicity, and organ damage is essential. Relapse is common. Prevention focuses on managing triggers like HBV infection.
b: Regular clinical assessment for disease flares.
Periodic assessment of organ function (renal, liver).
Vaccination against HBV for susceptible individuals.

t.b: Early detection of returning symptoms allows for prompt adjustment of therapy, preventing severe organ damage.
Prevents HBV infection, thereby reducing the risk of developing HBV-associated PAN in susceptible populations.

sections.p: PAN shares features with other systemic vasculitides and conditions causing multi-organ system disease, making differential diagnosis challenging. Key distinctions lie in the size of vessels involved and associated serological markers.

t.b: MPA typically affects smaller vessels and is often associated with MPO-ANCA. PAN affects medium vessels and is typically ANCA-negative.
SLE can cause multi-organ disease and vasculitis, but typically involves smaller vessels and is associated with specific autoantibodies (e.g., ANA, anti-dsDNA).

sections.p: Inflammatory markers can be normal in active PAN, and biopsy results can be falsely negative. Imaging may show non-specific changes. The absence of HBV markers does not rule out PAN.
b: Absence of HBV markers in some cases.

t.b: Can occur in patients with active PAN, especially if they are on corticosteroids. This can lead to underestimation of disease activity.
May occur if the sampled artery is not involved or if the inflammation is patchy. Clinical suspicion should guide further investigation.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute onset of neurological deficits (e.g., weakness, numbness, confusion)
Signs of gastrointestinal bleeding (e.g., hematemesis, melena)
Chest pain suggestive of myocardial infarction

faq.a: With prompt and aggressive treatment, remission can be achieved, and long-term control is possible, but it is often a chronic condition requiring ongoing management.

faq.q: Can herbal remedies cause Polyarteritis Nodosa?
faq.a: While not a direct cause, some herbal remedies can be hepatotoxic or interact with medications, potentially exacerbating underlying conditions or complicating management. Direct causation is rare.

faq.q: What is the prognosis for Polyarteritis Nodosa?
faq.a: Prognosis depends on the extent of organ involvement and response to treatment. Early diagnosis and treatment significantly improve outcomes, but severe disease can be life-threatening.

exam: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, and painful foot drop. His blood pressure is 170/100 mmHg. What are your top three differential diagnoses, and how would you differentiate them? — Differential diagnoses include PAN, systemic lupus erythematosus, and infective endocarditis. Differentiate using ANCA status, autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA), HBV serology, blood cultures, and imaging (angiography).

You suspect Polyarteritis Nodosa in a patient. What is the most crucial investigation to confirm the diagnosis, and what are its limitations? — Artery biopsy is the gold standard. Limitations include potential for false negatives if the affected vessel is not sampled or if inflammation is patchy.

Why is Hepatitis B serology so important in the workup of suspected Polyarteritis Nodosa? — Hepatitis B infection is a common identifiable trigger for PAN, leading to immune complex deposition. Identifying HBV allows for targeted antiviral therapy alongside immunosuppression.

A patient with suspected PAN has normal ESR and CRP. Should you rule out the diagnosis? — No. Inflammatory markers can be normal in active PAN, especially in patients already on corticosteroids. Clinical suspicion and other investigations remain paramount.

What are the immediate life-threatening complications of Polyarteritis Nodosa that require urgent intervention? — Mesenteric ischemia/infarction, renal artery stenosis leading to hypertensive crisis or acute kidney injury, myocardial infarction, and CNS vasculitis/stroke.

How does Polyarteritis Nodosa differ from microscopic polyangiitis? — PAN primarily affects medium-sized arteries and is typically ANCA-negative. Microscopic polyangiitis affects small vessels and is usually ANCA-positive (often MPO-ANCA).

If a patient has severe, life-threatening PAN, what immunosuppressive agent would you consider adding to corticosteroids, and why? — Cyclophosphamide. It is a potent immunosuppressant used for severe vasculitis to induce remission and prevent relapses by depleting B and T cells.

What role does angiography play in diagnosing Polyarteritis Nodosa? — Angiography (CT, MR, or conventional) can visualize characteristic findings such as aneurysms, stenoses, and occlusions in medium-sized arteries, strongly supporting the diagnosis of PAN.
